Neonates of the Long-tailed weasel, Mustela frenata, enter the world as altricial pups completely dependent on maternal care. Newborn individuals weigh just 3.1 grams [Wwb = 3.1 grams], a remarkably modest mass that underscores the species' altricial strategy. Gestation, during which the tiny embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis inside the uterus, lasts for approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days] when maternal body temperature is maintained near 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This relatively short intrauterine period is followed by an extended phase of lactation and maternal provisioning. The neonates are born with closed eyes and sparse fur, relying entirely on thermoregulation provided by the mother and the nest environment. Growth during the first few weeks is rapid, fueled by the mother's lipid-rich milk. The developmental trajectory of these altricial pups contrasts sharply with that of precocial mammalian neonates, which are mobile and capable of independent feeding shortly after parturition. Instead, Mustela frenata kits remain in the natal den for many weeks, sheltered from predators and environmental extremes while they accumulate somatic tissue and develop the sensory and motor capabilities necessary for eventual independent life.

Maternal investment continues intensively throughout the suckling juvenile stage as the young grow and develop. Under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of the active maternal metabolism, approximately 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the offspring reach the critical milestone of weaning at 37 days after birth [tx = 37 days after birth]. At this point, the individual kit has attained a wet weight of 34.6 grams [Wwx = 34.6 grams], reflecting nearly a tenfold increase from the 3.1 gram birth mass. The weaning process represents a significant dietary transition from exclusive milk consumption to the ingestion of solid prey items that the mother begins to bring to the den. This shift from nursing to solid food marks the onset of nutritional independence, though the young may continue to associate with the mother for some time, learning crucial hunting skills through observation and play. The substantial mass gain from birth to weaning indicates the efficiency of the mother's lactation strategy and the high energetic content of mustelid milk.

Sexual maturation in Mustela frenata exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing. Reaching puberty at 162 days after birth [tp = 162 days after birth], female kits are capable of breeding within their first calendar year, a life-history trait that facilitates rapid population turnover under favorable environmental conditions at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. In contrast, males require a substantially longer developmental period, achieving puberty at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This delayed maturation in males is likely driven by the energetic demands of attaining the larger body size necessary for successful territorial competition and mate acquisition. The differential timing of puberty between the sexes is a common pattern among carnivorans, often linked to polygynous or promiscuous mating systems where male reproductive success is contingent upon body size and social dominance. The extended juvenile period in males allows for continued somatic growth before the heavy energetic costs of intrasexual competition and scent-marking behavior begin to impose a significant metabolic burden.

The species exhibits a striking degree of sexual size dimorphism, a characteristic feature of many mustelids. Adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 290 grams [Wwi = approximately 290 grams], whereas adult males reach a considerably larger asymptotic mass of 450 grams [Wwi = 450 grams]. This difference has been well documented across the species' extensive geographic range, with males often being nearly twice as heavy as females. The dimorphism is most likely a product of sexual selection, where larger males enjoy a competitive advantage during the breeding season, while the smaller body size of females may confer energetic benefits related to reduced absolute food requirements and greater agility in pursuing small rodent prey through subterranean burrows. These body masses represent the asymptotic or near-asymptotic sizes for healthy, well-nourished adults; it is not uncommon for younger or reproductively stressed individuals to fall below these values. The extremes of these weights—roughly 85 to 267 grams for females and males combined—reflect the variation influenced by factors such as seasonal prey abundance, habitat quality, and latitude.

Reproductive output in the Long-tailed weasel is relatively modest compared to many small mammals but is consistent with its carnivorous, high-metabolic-rate lifestyle. Field studies indicate that females produce 6.2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 6.2 pups per litter], with typically just a single litter produced each year [F_R_i = single litter produced each year]. These events occur when ambient and maternal body temperatures approximate 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is just over eight years, a value derived from long-term mark-recapture studies and radiotelemetry data. This longevity, coupled with the relatively low annual reproductive rate, classifies Mustela frenata as a slow-reproducing, high-survival strategist within the mustelid family. The single annual litter limits the species' potential for rapid population irruption, but the extended lifespan of adults provides demographic stability across years with poor reproductive success, ensuring long-term population persistence even under fluctuating environmental conditions.
